item.title: Do I just care because they look like me?
item.description: The Tigray War killed hundreds of thousands. Four years later, Ethiopia is sliding back toward conflict.
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Jerusalem Demsas

The Tigray war, one of this century’s deadliest conflicts, killed an estimated 600,000 people from 2020 to 2022, and that may have only been the beginning.

At a very basic level, the Tigray War is a dispute between the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Ethiopian federal government, led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, over regional autonomy and political power. The TPLF and other subnational groups want to get rid of Abiy because of his efforts to centralize power. Some of these groups are divided over territory, even as they unite to oppose the federal government.

Hundreds of thousands of people died when the TPLF and the Ethiopian government went to war in 2020; while the Pretoria agreement negotiated in South Africa led to a short peace, key underlying disputes remain unresolved. They appear to be flaring up again now as both the federal government and the TPLF accuse each other of instigating the latest round of clashes this week. Even if the subnational groups succeed in getting rid of Prime Minister Abiy, the internal tensions are so strong that a brutal civil war is a likely outcome.

Most people know very little about the Tigray War. I would probably be one of them, except for the fact that I myself am ethnically Tigrayan. I was born just a few hundred miles away from Tigray’s capital, and when I look at the faces of the people involved — both those doing the killing and those being brutalized — they look like me.

At the same time, I live in the United States, speak broken Tigrinya in an inextinguishable American accent, and have no memories of my country of origin. Still, I have particular ties to the region and its people, so I care and know much more about Ethiopia than I otherwise would.

But you probably don’t. Many prominent political figures think this is good. While what’s happening in Ethiopia may be tragic, they argue, human beings are socially embedded creatures, which means that our obligations to other people are determined by the proximity of our relationships to them.

In January 2025, Vice President JD Vance sparked controversy by invoking the theological concept of ordo amoris (Latin for “order of love”) to claim that there is a hierarchy of obligation that requires you to care most about the people closest to you, in particular your family. Then, if there’s any room left over, you can give some consideration to people really far away from you. Vance argued that the far left has inverted this natural hierarchy to care more about people from other countries than people in its own — including, of course, migrants.

Pope Francis responded to this controversy by reaffirming the Catholic Church’s commitment to moral universalism: “Christians know very well that it is only by affirming the infinite dignity of all that our own identity as persons and as communities reaches its maturity. Christian love is not a concentric expansion of interests that little by little extend to other persons and groups.”

As a Protestant, I can empathize with Vance’s frustration at a man 4,500 miles away schooling him on his own religion, but I also think that’s exactly what you sign up for when you convert to Catholicism.

Alongside Vance-like arguments that we have few or no obligations to people outside our own communities is the argument that even empathizing with these people can be harmful. In The Atlantic, the Catholic writer Elizabeth Bruenig describes a growing right-wing literature warning against “toxic” and “suicidal” empathy. These books argue that indulging our empathy induces us to help vulnerable people at the expense of societal cohesion. As Bruenig points out, these books are targeted at conservatives who are torn between their concern for the poor and immigrants, on one hand, and their affiliation with a political party that increasingly rejects any obligation to marginalized groups on the other. It’s notable that some of the most active civil-society institutions aiding migrants are Christian organizations.

Empathy is a tool that helps us recognize the innate moral worth of every individual person, so it’s no surprise that people who seek to reject this moral fact are hostile to its power. However, it’s true that empathy can’t settle all our obligations. Because the world contains billions of people, my attention is selective. I pay attention to the Tigray War in part because I see my own features reflected in the faces of the participants. But that’s not the basis for a just or functional society.

There’s a soft form of particularism that is obviously true. I am a person who was born to a specific family in a specific place and therefore have special obligations to those people. If my father gets sick, my obligation to take care of him is greater than anyone else’s.

But when we move from explaining our duties to family and friends to relieving ourselves of obligations to other people, the particularist argument breaks down. If I were helping my dad deliver a package and a stranger collapsed in front of me, I think everyone would find it quite strange if I decided to ignore the dying man because of my preexisting duty to my family. In short, my obligation to care for my father does not, by itself, settle what I owe a stranger in desperate need.

Of course, recognizing that we owe something to strangers doesn’t tell us exactly what we owe them. I care a lot about what’s happening in Tigray, but that empathy doesn’t contain the answers to what the optimal immigration, foreign policy, or charitable arrangements are to relieve the suffering.

I don’t expect you to follow what happens in the Horn of Africa as closely as I do, nor does your lack of attention mean that you’re a bad, unempathetic person. Our personal connections can help us notice things that deserve everyone’s attention. My connection to Tigray helps explain why I know about its suffering, but the sheer scale of that suffering — hundreds of thousands of individual lives, each with innate moral worth — is the reason why it matters.

Midterm update

, our director of political data, uses data from The Argument’s polling operation to inform the Split Ticket 2026 House and Senate models. These models update every day; bookmark this page to see the odds of each party taking the House and the Senate.

Top stories this week, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

What do Hasan Piker, Hunter Biden’s memecoin, and convicted FTX fraudster Caroline Ellison’s return to the philanthropic world all have in common? They all suggest that society may be losing a useful taboo against associating with public figures who have demonstrated questionable ethics and judgment. This week, staff writer Jeremiah Johnson argues that we need to bring that taboo back.

The shift from phone- to web-based opinion polling has made high-integrity polling harder to do. It’s also made bad or outright fake polls far, far easier to produce. The result? Havoc in the epistemic commons. Pollster Charlotte Swasey analyzes the past decade in her industry so you can better understand your political news.

Should we be nice to AI? Personally, I think it’s worth trying, even if the odds are low that an AI is the kind of thing we owe moral consideration. But if we do want to be nice to AI, what thing should we even be kind to? The chatbot? The chips? It’s hard to know because “Claude” is really only the seamless orchestration of disparate unseen processes, just like a film is a bunch of still frames sped up past the point where we can see the gaps. Take a tour of an AI mind (if, indeed, such a mind exists) in my entry in our one-year anniversary series.

🌟Abundance Wins of the Week🌟

  • The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) finalized the design of a pilot process to speed up drug development. The program will pair drug makers with qualified research institutions to support their applications for first-in-human trials of new drugs. Instead of waiting for completed applications, the FDA will review application components piece by piece. The hope is to bring trial time down from its current two-year average and get closer to the faster timelines seen in China and Australia.

  • The United States Department of Energy selected 21 projects for up to $99 million in funding to explore next-generation geothermal drilling technology. One recipient is Fervo Energy, a company that also recently struck a deal with Google for the largest-ever geothermal project. So-called enhanced geothermal could provide abundant around-the-clock clean energy without the intermittent availability of solar and wind.

  • Just across the state line north of The Argument’s Washington, DC, headquarters, Maryland’s Montgomery County introduced a bill to make it easier to construct Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs). If passed, the law would remove both an owner-occupancy requirement and certain fees relating to ADU construction.

Worth watching…

Matt Yglesias is worried about AI doom. Jerusalem thinks that Terminator-style scenarios can distract us from more practical AI-related concerns, such as cybersecurity risk, economic fallout, and biological weapons. In other words, worrying about the end times might prevent us from seeing all the harms AI could cause along the way. So how much should you worry? And what exactly should you worry about? Tune in to sort it out for yourself.

Lakshya Jain, The Argument’s Director of Polling & Data, recently sat down with Adam Carlson from the polling firm Zenith Research to discuss projections for the upcoming midterms. Right now, all signs point to a massive swing toward Democrats. “I think earlier in the cycle, I was thinking a lot of things have to go right for Democrats,” Carlson told Jain. “Now I’m almost thinking the opposite, where a lot of things have to go well for Republicans to kind of keep this [blue wave] at bay.” Watch below to learn more.

In 2025, AI couldn’t beat the top high school students in the International Mathematical Olympiad, but this year, it’s solving open problems that no human mathematician has ever solved. Kai Williams, a reporter at Understanding AI, sat down with me discuss what this means not only for math but also for human achievement in other fields, as AI overtakes human abilities in new domains. Watch to find out.

What’s News with The Argument

The Argument recommends, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

Lately, these recommendation sections have had a consistent theme: Dolly Parton for the week of her passing; “birthdays” for the week of The Argument’s one-year anniversary. I greatly enjoyed the prompts, but I also thought it was time to pop the top button of the shirt collar, get loose, and leave things open-ended once again.

I asked my colleagues for “a recommendation,” plain and simple.

I did not expect the avalanche that would follow. My dear colleague , who’d just come back from a stint working from home, unleashed a torrent of kitchen-related recommendations. In a long string of Slack messages, he insisted on the centrality of the whetstone to the kitchen arsenal.

“Learn how to sharpen your knives in the kitchen!!” he implored.

Tracy also spent time in the kitchen, but her recommendation came through with the cutting parsimony of a Han Shan poem: “pickling a bunch of stuff at home.”

At this point, I realized a theme was emerging, despite my best intentions to suppress it. How do people work in unstructured space?

aligned with Angela’s exactness. He plucked out the very first line of the opening edition of a 1980s literary magazine he’s reading right now, called The Quarterly.

“The year I began to say vahz instead of vase,” its inaugural story, “The Harvest,” begins, “a man I barely knew nearly accidentally killed me.”

tended toward Milan’s overflowing grandeur in her assessment of the recent television series Furious. “I think a lot about gender — I’m the Gender & Culture fellow — but I think we all got desensitized to what sex trafficking really means in the post-Epstein era, and this show has called me out on how little I have conceptualized the actual crime,” she told me.

then tumbled into the chat, like a kid trying out his cannonball at the pool for the very first time.

“The End of Oak Street” he decreed. “It’s the Year of [Anne] Hathaway, so if you’re a Hathaway completist you need to see it!”

The Argument contributor chimed in to recommend Ghost in the Shell (“best movie about an AI safety incident!”) while his fellow Substacker lamented that Mad Men didn’t top Breaking Bad on The New York Times’ recent list of the top 100 TV shows of this century.

After all this, you may find the title of this week’s final recommendation, Stephen King’s Misery, to be fitting.

In the novel, a psychotic fan both rescues and tortures her favorite author. Jerusalem told us she “enjoyed King’s exploration of the writer’s desire to be taken seriously.” She thought King would portray the novel that Paul, the writer, wrote while being held captive by this super-fan as a bad work of art, “but the fact it produced a good novel says a lot about what [King] thinks keeps popular writers honest.”

There it was, an implicit exhortation to mind the ultimate judge, the ultimate jury, the ultimate constraint on open-ended-ness: the loyal fans (and readers) who keep you honest.

item.title: The least popular war since Vietnam
item.description: Trump’s war on Iran is dragging the whole Republican Party down
item.content:encoded:
By Lakshya Jain

Welcome back to The Argument’s poll series, where we survey Americans on the issues everyone’s fighting about. Our full crosstabs are available behind the paywall at the end of this post. Our last surveys have asked about elite perception, AI, crime, gender issues, and much more.

You can see every single poll published by The Argument here.

Our full methodology can be read here.

Before any politician makes a major policy change, they may want to ask themselves one simple question: Who are we helping with this?

Had Donald Trump asked himself that question before launching a war with Iran, he could have prevented what’s likely to become the biggest electoral cataclysm a political party has seen in a generation. New polling from The Argument shows that the conflict is even more toxic than George W. Bush’s war in Iraq, with only 33% of voters thinking it was right to enter, versus 55% saying it was wrong.

It’s not that the American electorate is reflexively opposed to military conflict. Our latest national poll found that a majority of registered voters think the U.S. would be justified in going to war in a variety of hypothetical cases — including one where the goal is to prevent a hostile country from obtaining a nuclear weapon. (That, of course, was the justification the administration gave for going to war with Iran.)

Share

But voters are not OK with this war. In fact, the conflict in the Middle East has been so disastrous for Republicans that it’s allowed Democrats to open up a 6-percentage-point lead in voter trust on foreign policy. That’s the biggest lead the party has held in the year we’ve been tracking this metric, and it’s up from the 1-point deficit it faced on this issue in May, before the ceasefire with Iran collapsed.

I could come up with any number of explanations for why this is the case. Memories of the Trump campaign’s vows to stay out of “forever wars” still ring fresh, and it seems likely that the anger Republicans face is the natural consequence of broken promises.

But fundamentally, I think Americans hate this war so much because of what it’s doing to their pocketbooks. It’s hard not to notice the inverse correlation that Trump’s approval rating has with gas prices. (It’s also important to point out that though this tracks with the empirical literature on the correlation between gas prices and approval, Trump is probably paying an outsized penalty because the price shock was a direct result of his specific actions.)

By itself, the deepening quagmire in the Middle East would be an unwelcome headache. But when it’s combined with a spiraling cost-of-living crisis, an unpopular trade war, and a chaotic and toxic immigration enforcement agenda, the picture is nothing short of disastrous for Republicans heading into the midterm elections. In fact, among likely voters, trust in Republicans now trails trust in Democrats on every single issue except crime.

There simply isn’t much good news for Republicans anywhere in our latest national survey. The president’s net approval sits 25 points underwater with registered voters and 26 points underwater with likely voters. These numbers make for an extraordinarily ugly contrast with 2018, when his net approval was “just” -9 in exit polls.

Though Democrats won the popular vote by 7 points and retook the House of Representatives in that election, today’s situation looks far more likely to yield a disaster for the Republican Party. Although the party “only” trails by 5.6 points with registered voters, this gap expands to 9 points with the likely 2026 electorate. (In some ways, I suppose Republicans are lucky it’s not even uglier, considering Trump’s approval is so much worse today than it was back then.)

It’s worth focusing on those generic ballot numbers for a second. If you were just to focus on the registered voter numbers, Republicans would actually be doing a bit better than they were in 2018. But not all of these people are going to vote, and considering the demographics, voting history, and self-reported enthusiasm of each voter allows us to more precisely estimate the population that is actually likely to vote. After factoring that in, Democrats open up a gaping lead on the congressional ballot, bolstering their advantage by more than 3 points.

In other words, though persuasion is a critical part of the story, the thing that takes this from a “blue wave” to a “blue tsunami” is the significant enthusiasm gap between the two sides.

Subscribe now

For a while, Republican leaders have hoped that Democrats would be dragged down by perceptions that the party is too far to the left. As recently as this summer, in fact, they might have been justified in this expectation. Republicans were actually perceived as less extreme than Democrats in our July poll. Back then, 47% of likely voters said the Democratic Party was too far to the left, while 45% said the Republican Party was too far to the right.

But now the environment has deteriorated so badly for Republicans that this is no longer true.

In a stark reversal from our results a year ago, the Republican Party is now also considerably more unpopular than the Democratic Party.

As a result, Democratic odds of taking the Senate have never looked better, with deep-red states like Iowa, Kansas, and Nebraska moving into play as Republican strength in the Midwest evaporates. Combined with a rebellion among Hispanic voters and a polling lead that Mary Peltola continues to hold in Alaska, Republicans find themselves outright underdogs in the Senate for the first time in the cycle.

This was unthinkable a year ago, given that Democrats have to flip at least two seats in states Trump won by double digits in 2024.

Pundits and analysts alike have a tendency to overdetermine results after they have happened and tell the story of an election with far more confidence than that story really deserved. But let me be clear: The current unpopularity of the Republican Party is the result of a series of entirely avoidable actions taken by the president. Trump entered office as popular as ever, and he has proceeded to summarily squander that popularity through a sequence of unforced errors.

It was a choice to deploy Immigration and Customs Enforcement to Minneapolis, kick-starting a needless firestorm after three poorly trained agents shot two innocent Americans dead. It was a choice to levy incredibly unpopular tariffs and start an inflationary trade war during a cost-of-living crisis. And it was a choice to attack Iran and send gasoline prices skyrocketing during a time when Americans already felt stretched financially.

Our survey isn’t without glimmers of hope for Republicans. It’s still possible for them to keep the Senate if a systematic polling error happens. Polls in 2020 and 2016 far overstated the Democratic margin due to a systematic undersampling of low-propensity voters. Though we employ a lot of sophisticated survey guards to ward against this very thing (like including respondents who begin taking our surveys but drop off before completing them, a far less Democratic-swinging group than the other respondents), we can’t ever fully rule out the possibility of an error.1

If the war ends, gas prices dip, and the Republicans’ considerable cash edge begins to dent the image of Democratic candidates, it is conceivable that the party could claw back some of the ground it lost throughout this process. But that would require a series of actions that the president has not expressed interest in taking.

Without a serious and sudden reversal in fortune, Trump is about to send his political party off of an electoral cliff.

Upgrade to a paid subscription today to get access to the full crosstabs!

METHODOLOGY NOTE

Our poll was fielded between Sept. 16 and 22, 2026. We surveyed 1,603 registered voters across the nation; 1,533 completed the survey, while 70 partial responses completed at least until the generic congressional ballot question, where they were asked which party’s candidate they intended to vote for in November.

The sample was weighted to be representative of the universe of registered voters in the United States by race; age; gender; education; census region; race by gender; age by gender; race by education; modeled presidential partisanship by age, education, and gender; and 2024 vote choice. Questions up until the generic congressional ballot were weighted including partial interviews, and then questions after the generic ballot were weighted separately to the same parameters, but using only the complete interviews.

The margin of sampling error was plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. The design effect of the survey, which measures the loss of statistical precision due to weighting and design, was 1.22. Accounting for the design effect, the full margin of error was plus or minus 2.7 percentage points.

This iteration of The Argument’s national survey produces estimates of both registered and likely voters for the 2026 midterm elections. The likely voter screen takes every respondent’s demographic and voting history and calculates a probability that they will vote in 2026. It then aligns this with probabilistic turnout scores from self-expressed vote likelihood and rakes this to the likely 2026 electorate, calculated via historic demographic turnout data from a Catalist voter file sample, in order to estimate their likelihood of voting.

This survey was designed and weighted by The Argument. Data collection was performed by Verasight, and voter file data and weighting targets were obtained from Catalist. A full methodology statement is available on the last page of the survey PDF. A detailed explanation of how our surveys work is available here.

Thanks to Josh Kalla, Amanda Iovino, Guy Molyneaux, Charlotte Swasey, and Carroll Doherty for reviewing this month’s polling language. As part of The Argument’s polling advisory committee, these experts have provided comments to ensure the rigor and objectivity of this polling project. They are not responsible for the ultimate language choices made by The Argument, and all errors are our own.

Subscribe now

item.title: Stop trying to make xenophobia sound smart
item.description: No one actually cares about how immigration impacts the economy
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

This week on The Argument podcast, Matt Yglesias and I talk about the rise of the far right in Europe. Paid subscribers can watch or listen to the episode ad free here and read the transcript at the end of this post. Free subscribers can watch the episode on YouTube here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Lots of people don’t like immigrants. I remember, as a young child growing up in a very progressive city in suburban Maryland, a woman telling my family to “go back to where you came from.” From my (albeit flawed) childhood memory, the proximate cause of her distress was the limited seating at the Barnes & Noble Starbucks, but my mother’s accent tipped her over into xenophobia.

As a real abundance-head, my first instinct is to point out that scarcity can activate these sorts of insider-outsider dynamics in even the most trivial settings. If there were enough tables and chairs for everyone to sit comfortably, there would never have been any conflict over the scarce resources.

But while it’s true that this woman would likely have been annoyed and maybe even outwardly rude to a white, seemingly native-born family, it’s unlikely that she would have seen them as less deserving of Starbucks table space. That’s because there is a widespread underlying belief that longstanding membership as part of a nation or state or town makes you a more legitimate member of that community.

The first thing to say is that this belief is incorrect. Having lived somewhere longer does not make you more deserving of ordinary respect, fair treatment, human rights, or a seat at the combination Starbucks-Barnes & Noble. People do not acquire superior moral standing simply because one of their ancestors arrived somewhere earlier.

Share

But the second thing to say is that most people seem to disagree with me. Unfortunately, due to a combination of bad reasoning and different values, many people think that accidents of birth are a just way of allocating rights.

I expect that most of the people reading this piece are relatively cosmopolitan individuals who find it sort of embarrassing that so many people in their coalitions hold beliefs like these. But that’s the world we live in. And it’s a problem that many thought leaders grasp for highbrow rationalizations that make these indisputably lowbrow views sound like conclusions compelled by economic research.

We have to be able to reckon with the fact that winning a democratic election means dealing with the fact that some people dislike immigration for no good reason without torturing logic and social science research to justify such views.

It takes a lot of effort to make immigration look zero-sum

As anti-immigration politics has roiled Western nations, elites have grasped for rationalizations of xenophobia in order to co-opt anti-immigration politics without obviously abandoning their commitments to empiricism and cosmopolitanism. In so doing, they have begun to distort economic reasoning to try to justify ideas like Immigration reduces wages for the native-born and, increasingly, Immigrants are a fiscal drag.

The idea that immigrants reduce native-born wages is so difficult to produce evidence for that its boosters have to resort to looking at sub-sub-groups like “non-Hispanic men without high school diplomas” to find even the slightest effects. For instance, the famous result from economist George Borjas’ paper on the Mariel Boatlift, which brought a wave of Cuban immigrants to Miami, is that the boatlift led to 10% to 30% wage declines among 25- to 59-year-old non-Hispanic high school dropouts.

Other economists later found that the survey behind Borjas’ famous study began sampling a larger share of Black workers around the same time that the refugees arrived. Because Black workers already earn less on average, that is a likely explanation of the apparent wage decline among this subgroup.

To accept that Borjas was right about the wage effects on this subgroup, you also have to ignore the tiny sample (an average of 19.5 per year), the suspicious fact that similar effects do not appear if female or Hispanic workers are included, and that the effect disappears if slightly different age ranges are used or if high school graduates are included.

His work also has nothing to say about the fact that these same workers benefited from expanded output and lower prices as a result of the boatlift.

And that’s before you consider the lion’s share of studies that find that immigration does not make native-born workers worse off.

This wage argument is still around, but the new smart anti-immigration take isn’t about native-born wages; it’s about whether immigrants are a net drain on government coffers. As the Financial Times’ John Burn-Murdoch recently wrote: “concerns about the economic impacts of immigration on high-income countries have shifted from fears that incomers are taking the jobs of existing residents to worries that the low (or no) pay of arrivals will place a growing financial burden on the host country.”

In the U.S., Vice President JD Vance has argued that unauthorized immigration plus generous benefits would “bankrupt this country more than any other policy.”

In the U.K., a (then) prominent Conservative Party leadership candidate argued that each person arriving illegally “costs the taxpayer roughly £400,000 over their lifetime.”

The fiscal argument has gained traction among mainstream journalists with substantial sway in liberal circles. In a now-viral chart produced by The Economist, migrants from the Middle East, North Africa, Pakistan, and Turkey appear as a net drain on Denmark’s government spending at every point in their lives.

It is straightforwardly true that if you make it very difficult to work as a newcomer (as many European countries do) and then make it very easy to get benefits (as many European countries also do), then the net fiscal cost will be higher.

But those fiscal costs would then be a direct result of policy choices that countries could easily change — for instance, the United States does not extend the same level of universal benefits to noncitizens, and it also makes it easier for them to work. But also, most of the studies that these claims rely on just do not prove that immigrants are a net cost!

Subscribe now

Burn-Murdoch relies on new research from Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research’s Usama Polani to illustrate the fiscal costs of low-earning couples in France, Spain, Germany, and the United Kingdom. The paper calculates the government revenue attributed to migrant households (mostly taxes they pay) and subtracts the government spending on them (everything from welfare benefits to shares of public goods).

Polani, to his credit, acknowledged his study’s limitations and admirably incorporated corporate taxes that do account for some of the indirect fiscal benefits of immigration. But even that still misses large pathways by which immigrants contribute to the tax base like the effects on other residents’ wages and labor supply.

These graphs do a bunch of argumentative work by giving readers a salary threshold below which an immigrant family costs taxpayers money on net under the model’s assumptions. It’s totally fine to do this as an academic accounting exercise, but the obvious takeaway to a general audience is that immigrants cost the taxpayers more than they contribute.

That is not actually true.

Fundamentally, if you’re trying to understand the impact of a person on government coffers, you can’t just hold everything else constant. New people are not just consumers of government benefits and producers of taxes — they are also both consumers and producers of goods and services.

Increased demand for goods and services induces companies to make more products, which means hiring more people and investing more capital. That, in turn, produces more income and corporate taxes.

Another indirect fiscal benefit comes when immigrants provide childcare, allowing a parent to work more hours or even re-enter the workforce. This increases the taxes received by the government.

These are not mere hypotheticals; research has found that immigration stimulates business investment, allows high-earning women to spend more time in paid work, and generates indirect fiscal benefits through its effects on other residents’ wages and employment.

When you are thinking about the fiscal costs and benefits of immigration, you can’t just look at a simple accounting exercise; you have to actually ask the question: What would the fiscal situation look like with and without immigration?

Overlooking this broader context is depressingly common in debates on the fiscal effects of immigration. In 2023, economist Michael Clemens published a paper showing that when you account for the increased corporate taxes collected by the government, the net fiscal impact of average recent U.S. immigrants rose by a factor of 3.2, with a much smaller gap between the net contributions of highly educated and less-educated immigrants. Even average recent immigrants with less than a high school education are net positive!

A 2024 economics paper estimated the indirect fiscal effects of low-skilled immigration through changes in existing residents’ wages and labor supply. It found that in the U.S. context, these immigrants each produce an indirect fiscal benefit of roughly $750 annually on average. The mechanism is that low-skilled immigrants raise wages of workers whose skills complement theirs: More construction workers can raise wages for construction managers, for instance. That means those construction managers earn more and pay more in taxes.1

Another example of fiscal benefits of immigration came from a 2024 Congressional Budget Office report that modeled projections of the deficit with and without the immigration surge from 2021 to 2026. The projected federal budget deficit from 2024 to 2034 was roughly $900 billion lower than it would have been without the new residents.

Subscribe now

I don’t have direct proof that anyone’s commitment to these highbrow rationalizations is insincere. But I will say that I have yet to see anyone have the courage of their convictions when it comes to the idea that we should reject new people if they are a net fiscal cost to the government.

If any of the fiscal-costs truthers took their own logic seriously, that would mean the average birth was a net fiscal drag on any government currently running deficits. After all, if the government is spending more than it is bringing in, that means the average person is taking more than they are giving. Time for mass sterilization!2

Accept reality. There are dumb and wrong people who get to vote.

There is more that countries can do — particularly in Europe — to make sure labor markets are prepared to absorb new people in order to maximize the economic benefits and minimize the fiscal costs. And they should do those things!

As Alexander Kustov and my colleague Kelsey Piper wrote earlier this year, one reason why America is so much better at assimilating immigrants is that “Europe makes it structurally much harder for immigrants to work. Rigid employment protection, sector-wide collective bargaining, and high effective minimum wages create insider-outsider dynamics that hit newcomers hardest.”

But even if countries do make needed changes, there will still be a lot of people in Western liberal democracies who neither understand nor seem to care very much that immigration is clearly an economic benefit. The important objections to immigration come in three categories: crime, disorder, and culture.

Consider what happens when immigrants obviously pass every economic test. In a recent discussion of “The Indian Question,” the Manhattan Institute’s Christopher Rufo pointed out that Indians have high rates of college matriculation and earnings, but he nevertheless offered a highbrow rationalization for preferring a homogeneous society because of “higher trust, higher cooperation.” His co-host, the popular right-wing commentator Lomez, argued that preferring an ethnically homogeneous country doesn’t need an economic justification, comparing it to preferring one food over another.

In polling conducted by The Argument, pluralities of respondents told us that they believed immigration had a positive impact economically, culturally, and overall. The only place that a greater share of respondents reported negative effects was public safety.

We even asked whether forcing immigrants to pay higher taxes — a policy I have supported! — would get respondents to support more legal immigration. Just 9% of voters said yes to this. In contrast, 52% said that “close vetting of immigrants to prevent criminals and terrorists from entering” would make them more comfortable with “increasing the number of legal immigrants admitted each year.” Notably, this is also irrational given that immigrants commit way less crime than native-born Americans do on a per-capita basis!

In today’s episode of The Argument, my co-host Matt Yglesias argues that I’m not sympathetic to the plight of the white moderate who is struggling to reconcile the electorate’s discomfort with immigration with their own personal cosmopolitanism.

“This is my criticism of you,” he argues. “I think you don’t engage sympathetically with the dilemma that people, especially white Americans who are trying to nudge Democrats into a more politically pragmatic view on immigration, face. Because if you say, ‘We need to pander to the racism of the electorate,’ people are going to say, ‘Nope, that’s not allowed,’ right?”

I separate my advice into two parts. First, to people who are in truth-seeking roles in academia, journalism, and think tanks: Attempts to find smart-person reasons for why everyone’s mad at immigration risk polluting the elite epistemic environment without resolving any of the concerns that real anti-immigration voters have.

Second, to politicians: I do not think you should say that we should pander to racists, and I don’t think taking bigotry seriously means capitulating to it.

Instead, immigration advocates like myself should focus on the following: reducing the amount of zero-sum competition that pits native-born citizens and immigrants against one another, taking crime very seriously and holding a hard line against immigrants who commit crimes, investing in orderly immigration processes to eliminate irregular border encounters, and demanding cultural assimilation from newcomers.

Taking these substantive concerns seriously is ultimately better for the pro-immigration cause and more respectful to the democratic views of immigration-skeptical voters than torturing the empirical literature to rationalize the false view that immigration is a resource-draining, zero-sum competition.

Matt and I talk about all this, plus unrelated reasons that the far right is rising in Europe, on this week’s podcast.

By Jerusalem Demsas

We’re thrilled to open applications for the second cohort of The Argument Fellowship, a yearlong, full-time program designed to train the next generation of opinion journalists.

Fellows in our program learn to pitch, report, and write on a dedicated beat under the guidance of our senior editorial staff. They participate in regular lectures and workshops with leading thinkers and practitioners.

This year, our fellows Kobe Yank-Jacobs, Maibritt Henkel, and Milan Singh probed topics like nationalizing AI labs, factionalism in the Democratic Party, and how we should interpret the U.S. fertility rate. Beyond the written word, they livestreamed interviews with thought leaders and produced videos on our core coverage areas.

In workshops throughout the year, our fellows learned from government professor Hans Noel on the evolution of political parties, legal scholar David Schleicher on reporting about housing policy, economist Michael Clemens on immigration, reporter Rachel Cohen Booth on building a career in journalism, and economist Oliver Kim on global development (to name a few).

If you’re an early career writer who is excited by these kinds of questions, opportunities, and debates, this opportunity is for you! If you know someone who might be a good fit, please share this post.

Share

Program Overview

Based in The Argument’s Washington, D.C., newsroom, fellows will work closely with editors to develop the skills, discipline, and intellectual range needed to succeed in opinion journalism.

Over the course of the year, fellows will:

  • Produce a regular volume of published work, learning to pitch, report, and refine ideas into polished commentary.

  • Co-author our Sunday post, The Closing Argument.

  • Participate in events such as Substack Live conversations.

  • Produce social and video multimedia content.

  • Receive hands-on editorial mentorship and feedback from senior editors.

  • Participate in regular lectures featuring leading journalists, scholars, and practitioners.

  • Engage in workshops on interviewing, data literacy, story framing, and self-editing.

Each fellow will be assigned one or more focus areas, like:

  • Abundance and economic policy

  • Gender, families, and culture

  • Technology and society

  • Polling and political analysis

Who Should Apply

We’re looking for early-career writers — typically with one to two years of professional or academic experience — who are eager to develop as opinion journalists. You might be a recent graduate or someone working in a field like housing, energy, tech, or policy who wants to translate that expertise into journalism.

Ideal candidates will have:

  • Strong writing and analytical skills.

  • Curiosity about politics, policy, and culture.

  • The ability to synthesize complex ideas clearly and persuasively.

  • An openness to feedback and collaboration.

  • A demonstrated interest in public debate and persuasion.

You don’t need prior newsroom experience — just the drive to think critically, write clearly, and engage deeply with ideas.

Compensation and Details

  • Location: Washington, D.C. (in-person)

  • Duration: January to December 2027

  • Salary: $50,000 per year

  • Benefits: Healthcare coverage support included

How to Apply

Email jobs@theargumentmag.com with the subject line: “The Argument Fellowship Application — [Your Name]”

Please include:

  • Resume

  • Cover letter (explain why you’re a good fit, rank your preferred focus areas, and share two story ideas with reporting plans)

  • One to two writing samples that demonstrate analytical or argumentative skill

  • Two to three references

  • Two pieces of content that you’ve valued even though you disagreed with them (article, podcast, book, movie, or other piece of art)

Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis.

Short-listed candidates will complete a paid work test assessing writing, analytical, and editorial judgment skills. You will have 90 minutes to complete a short brief based on provided materials. This is designed to evaluate how you think, argue, and write under deadline.

item.title: MAGA is having a normal one
item.description: Also: The online stans-turned-political-prisoners and ...is Threads back?
item.content:encoded:
By Jeremiah Johnson

Welcome to The Weekly Scroll!

The Weekly Scroll is a once-a-week roundup of the most interesting, strangest, and funniest stories from around the social internet.

This week, we’re talking about the online Right’s collective freakout, how Threads still hasn’t become a thing, and why stan accounts keep ending up as political prisoners.

The Right’s no-good, very bad week

It’s not the best time to be a MAGA soldier online. Poll after poll shows that Democrats are massive favorites to take back a majority in the House of Representatives next month, and they’re increasingly viewed as favorites to take back the Senate as well. The Argument/Split Ticket model currently gives Democrats an 89% chance of winning the House, and a 61% chance of taking the Senate. Trump’s approval is now at -26 with likely voters. It’s hard out there!

Surely the online Right has cooked up some fantastic responses, right? What have the loyal patriots of the MAGA machine been doing as the electorate turns on them?

Well, Chris Rufo — the Manhattan Institute fellow famous for kicking off the right’s war on critical race theory — decided to devote a full episode of his podcast to “The Indian Question.” The “question” at hand is literally just the existence of Indian Americans and whether or not white people should feel disgusted by them. I watched the entire 72-minute podcast so you don’t have to (and you gremlins better subscribe to The Argument because god knows I’m not doing that for free), and it’s as bad as you’d suspect something echoing the Jewish Question would be.

Rufo, along with his co-host Jonathan Keeperman — better known as @L0m3z on Twitter, where he’s argued that best response to the left is “shut up fag“ — argued at various points that Indians can never assimilate as long as anyone can notice that they’re different, that racism against non-white Americans is actually good because it’s a form of “hazing,” and that meritocracy is probably a flawed idea because Indians keep winning the spelling bee.

Subscribe now

The typical exchange is Rufo trying to launder white nationalist talking points with some more reasonable-sounding justification, followed by an objection from Keeperman that no, let’s be very clear, we just think the Indians are gross and don’t need to have a reason why. Rufo then typically gives a little “this crazy guy!” grin, concedes the point and moves on. I wish I was making any of this up.

Keeperman: There are a lot of people for whom… the preference to live in a homogeneous society… there’s not like some rational reason necessarily for it. They just like it better in the way that certain people like certain kinds of foods better. They don’t owe a kind of reasoned explanation for why they prefer a slice of pizza to a burrito or something.

Which makes sense, because being disgusted by another race of person is exactly like preferring pizza to burritos.

The episode drew significant pushback in conservative circles, probably because it was 25% too open about the kind of white nationalism that lurks under the surface of so much modern right-wing politics. But Rufo’s podcast wasn’t the only racial controversy this week — the right also had a miniature war over whether or not it was anti-white racism for Sarah Huckabee Sanders to air an ad depicting a white man on welfare.

And far-right Twitter personality @Howlingmutant0 — best known for racist, misogynistic, and antisemitic jokes that have attracted the attention of followers like Vice President JD Vance — was stunned that after years of cultivating a fanbase of white nationalists, he faced a revolt from that fanbase after it was revealed he has a mixed-race child.

But hey! This is all just internet stuff, podcasts and influencers. Maybe right-wingers in office are doing better.

Jack Smith, the former special counsel in charge of investigating Donald Trump, was on the Hill this week to defend his scrutiny of the president before Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee. The title of the hearing was “Oversight of Jack Smith’s Abuse of Authority and the Targeting of Republicans and Related Matters.”

It all went south for Republicans during questioning by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., whose inquiries about whether Smith attended an Atlanta Hawks basketball game completely fell apart.

The questioning was meant to somehow establish that Smith had improper ties to Georgia prosecutor Fani Willis, who indicted Trump in a separate state case over alleged efforts to overturn the 2020 election. Schmitt is visibly grinning to himself during the exchange, revealing texts Smith’s staff sent about attending a basketball game.“I don’t think you know that we have this stuff,” Schmitt says smugly before accusing Smith of perjury.

What a bombshell!1 But wait! It turns out that some poor staffer made a mistake. They either forgot that women’s basketball exists, or confused the Atlanta Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes, as Smith confirmed that he was actually at a women’s college basketball game between Maryland and Iowa, and nowhere near Atlanta.

The moment was so humiliating it spawned the first ever Congressional Surrender Cobra.2

What makes the entire thing so funny is how utterly confident Schmitt was that he had a major, blockbuster scandal to reveal. It’s common to build a press strategy to try and amplify big moments in Congress. Right as Schmitt’s line of questioning was falling apart, conservative influencers were tweeting seemingly pre-prepared talking points. After the hearing, Schmitt had a recording of the Charlie Kirk Podcast lined up to celebrate his big win, and bumbled his way through it without ever acknowledging he got the only fact that mattered completely wrong. And Schmitt had, just that morning, been pumped up by Axios as a potential VP candidate for 2028. RIP to Schmitt’s VP chances (Born Sept 29th, died Sept 29th).

Things went no better on Pennsylvania Avenue: The White House deputy chief of staff posted a six-second clip that may have been thinly veiled QAnon signalling while the president tried to rebrand AI as SI (superintelligence).3

But this is all dude stuff — I bet at least the right’s women are being normal! Haha, no, the big women’s stories out of MAGA this week are a conspiracy that Candace Owens is a secret lesbian and an article about an anti-feminist “groypette” who was shocked, shocked when her groypers turned on her.

Why is MAGA being overrun by scandals, insane nonsense, and infighting? This is what happens when a party is facing electoral disaster and knows it. The political media is having a field day writing article after article about Republican midterm panic. The war with Iran remains toxically unpopular, the price of gas is still high, and there’s little good news to focus on. Small wonder that the online right is collapsing into failed conspiracy theories, racist nonsense, and back-stabbing.

Gaga Daily was in jail

The X account @GaGaDaily was like any other popular stan account: posting videos, memes, and more about Lady Gaga to an audience of almost half a million followers. But in February of 2024, the account suddenly went silent for more than a year. Now, we finally know what happened:

The New York Times has more detail — the account belongs to a Belarussian man named Kirill, who was arrested in February 2024 for participating in 2020 anti-government protests. He spent two years in a Belarussian prison before being released, and he now lives abroad. Lady Gaga, disappointingly, has not commented.

Oddly, this isn’t the first time a stan account creator has found themselves jailed for geopolitical stances. In 2019, a Taylor Swift fan account announced they’d been inactive for about two months because they were jailed for refusing to join the Israeli Defense Forces.

Subscribe now

Stop trying to make Threads happen

These days, there’s a specific type of story that gets written a couple of times per year. I don’t know if there’s a Central Bureau of Promoting Threads or if it’s just irresistible, but every so often, we get the “guys, Threads is really happening this time!” article. This week, it’s from Wired, who declares that Black Twitter is thriving on Threads.

For some reason, journalists keep trying to make this particular brand of fetch happen. They point out that Threads hit 500 million monthly active users this summer. They compare it to Reddit. They seem very eager for Threads to break out.

Yes, Threads has a lot of “users.” But while that metric is kind of real, it’s also kind of fake. Threads is heavily integrated with Instagram and Facebook, and many of its “active users” are people who accidentally click through to Threads content while on those other apps. The hottest meme on Threads this summer was “Richard has passed,” which is a joke about how lots of Facebook users are posting on Threads without even realizing they’re doing it.

So while Threads technically has users, it seems to be a fully vaporware userbase. They don’t spend any time there. Check out this graph of average daily time spent by active Android-app users by social network:

Threads is losing to Pinterest and LinkedIn!

More than just not being an app where people spend any real amount of time, Threads also doesn’t generate culture. Love it or hate it, Twitter is still essential for understanding online culture and politics, and it still has a remarkable density of people whose posts go on to become major news cycles or generate cultural discourse. Threads has none of that. The quality of content there is so bad that the tech writer Max Read dubbed it the “gas-leak social network.”

That’s probably why only 3% of Americans say they get news from Threads, a number so low that it runs into the Lizardman’s Constant. When was the last time someone showed you an awesome Threads meme? When was the last time an important cultural moment happened on Threads? Has it ever? I’m begging you all, stop. Stop trying to make Threads happen. It’s not going to happen.

Links

  • TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama $100 million in another instance of a social media company settling with a state government over claims of social media harms to children. As part of the settlement, TikTok also agreed to a number of product changes like time limits for teens, nighttime usage restrictions, a default non-personalized feed, and a ban on cosmetic filters for teens.

  • Pop singer Sia has sold a 50% stake in her musical catalog for $180 million. These deals are becoming more and more popular, and are part of a phenomenon I’ve written about before: Older, previously released art is smothering new art.

  • The Hollywood Reporter, in addition to tracking broadcast TV, streaming hits, and box office grosses, is now tracking the internet’s most popular microdramas.

  • I have been having an unreasonable amount of fun playing “Unusual Suspects”, a game where you do police sketches of various fictional characters.

  • Mattel released a “Hanukkah Barbie,” and it went poorly.

  • Caleb Hammer’s humiliation economy

Posts

  • A very good cat costume

  • Historical reenactment

  • Woke university

  • Who cares about existential risk anyway?

  • Are you wearing…

Subscribe now

1

Sidenote: It’s not even clear what this ‘bombshell’ would have proven. That Smith and Fani Willis were … in the same city on the same day? Okay?

2

I also strongly recommend this incredible view of Alabama Senator Katie Britt, who looks like she’s having ‘Nam flashbacks as she realizes what’s happening.

3

It’s also been alleged that insiders may have scooped up prominent .si domain names ahead of the announcement.

item.title: Americans want Congress to stop the imperial presidency
item.content:encoded:
By Kobe Yank-Jacobs

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

According to both President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, what the U.S. military is doing in Iran is not a war. That said, as of Friday, the U.S. is moving an additional 10,000 troops and a third aircraft carrier to the region, raising concerns that this suspiciously warlike “conflict” could escalate.

By all accounts, Americans are sick of the conflict, which was started unilaterally by the president. According to new data, they are also ready for Congress to rein it in.

Sixty-six percent of registered voters in The Argument’s latest poll, fielded nationally between September 16th and 22nd, believe that the president should be required to get Congressional approval before sending armed forces into action — and only 21% oppose. Almost a majority would go even further: 50% of voters believe that Congress should defund a military action when the president moves ahead without Congressional approval. (Only 26% of respondents oppose this.) Historically, the main enabler of unilateral presidential warmaking has been legislators’ skittishness about reigning in conflicts after they’ve started, but our survey suggests that this is a step that voters feel they are entitled to take.

Subscribe now

Now, it would be great if this result was motivated by high-minded respect for the Constitution, which is very clear that Congress is the branch with the power “to declare war,”1 but a closer look at the results suggests the results are heavily influenced by current events. For one, the current war in Iran — initiated unilaterally by President Trump — is the most unpopular war since Vietnam, when compared to Afghanistan, Iraq, and World War II. More voters think that George W. Bush’s invasion of Iraq was justified than the current conflict.

There is also a strong partisan slant to our poll results: 94% of people who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 said they think that Congress should approve war, while only 40% of Trump voters said the same. That said, 44% of Trump voters ages 30 to 44 preferred requiring Congressional approval, suggesting younger generations may be closer to consensus on the need for Congressional approval.2

But even if our results reflect anxieties specific to this moment in time, the overwhelming support for Congressional signoff is still a rebuke of what’s become business-as-usual in Washington.

The United States has not actually declared war since World War II. Beginning with the Korean War in 1950, presidents have either ordered troops into combat unilaterally, secured a different form of wartime “authorization” (as George W. Bush did to invade Afghanistan), or plainly abused past authorizations to make war elsewhere. (The Afghanistan authorization was used to justify drone strikes in Yemen and Somalia.) The result is that presidents functionally make war wherever and whenever they want.

In 1991, when asked what he would do if Congress declined to authorize the Gulf War, President George H.W. Bush told a reporter, “I still feel that I have the constitutional authority” — a sentiment later echoed by presidents from Barack Obama to Donald Trump.3

Thankfully, we don’t necessarily need high-minded Constitutionalism to change how things are done. Some of the most substantial reforms to presidential authority have come in response to specific presidents violating a norm or law, including term limits (after FDR), anti-nepotism laws (after JFK), and restrictions on withholding congressionally appropriated funds (after Nixon).

Congressional capitulation

The fact that half of registered voters are open to Congress taking action even after a president moves ahead with a war unilaterally could be the key to reigning in the executive here.

Once presidents take the initiative to launch a combat operation, it’s hard for politicians in Congress to take a vote opposing or reversing it. There is a fundamental asymmetry between a single person with the ability to handle threats quickly and a large deliberative body, lumbering along in its approval, each politician fearful of being seen as unpatriotic. That’s how war powers got out of whack in the first place: The history of U.S. warmaking is the president using dramatic incidents — real or provoked or lied about — to cow Congress into going along.

As early as 1846, James Polk ordered troops into disputed territory between the Nueces River and the Rio Grande to provoke the start of the Mexican-American War. To stir up support for the Spanish-American war in 1898, President William McKinley pointed to the explosion of a ship off the coast of Havana, despite inconclusive evidence about the cause of the explosion. (Later evidence has suggested it may have been an internal issue, not an attack).

In the summer of 1964, the Johnson administration claimed that its ships were innocently patrolling international waters when struck by the North Vietnamese, but they were really 12 miles off the Vietnamese coast, likely trying to draw fire. (The second of the alleged strikes also never happened.)

The modern era has made this dynamic — presidents making war a fait accompli and daring Congress to pull them back — much worse. In 1973, in the waning days of the Vietnam War, Congress tried to restrain presidents by passing the War Powers Resolution. The law generally required presidents to get congressional approval within 60 days or end hostilities, with up to 30 additional days if necessary for a safe withdrawal. But presidents have used that deadline to justify acting unilaterally.

Unfortunately, the law has had the opposite of its intended effect. On paper, it cemented the requirement for Congressional signoff. In practice, it gave presidents the green light for monthslong deployments that sitting members of Congress would end up hesitant to rein in.

The real significance of The Argument’s finding, even if it was heavily motivated by the current war on Iran, may be that the public believes Congress can act forcefully after a president has initiated combat, which is where we most need Congress to be muscular. If the issue is that legislators find it politically untenable to go against a war once it’s started, we now know that, in the abstract at least, the public is on their side.

The founders understood that excessive warmaking would not be due to the flawed character of this or that president but endemic to the office. That’s why they gave the power to Congress. It just so happens that this separation of powers is especially important when a president with a flawed character does take the helm.

Subscribe now

Midterm update

Lakshya Jain, our director of political data, uses data from The Argument’s polling operation to inform the Split Ticket 2026 House and Senate models. Here’s his update on the state of play this week:

Democrats remain the firmest of favorites to win the House, thanks to an environment that is even more favorable than it was in 2018: Their win probability is 89%. In the Senate, Democrats have a slight edge, with a 60% chance of winning the chamber thanks to leads in Alaska, Texas, Ohio, and North Carolina. Maine and Iowa are both tossup races, but Democrats only need to flip four of these six to take the chamber. Right now, polling and fundamentals are both so good for them that they’ve got a better-than-even chance of doing exactly that.

These models update every day; bookmark this page to see the odds of each party taking the House and the Senate.

Top stories this week, by Milan Singh

Nikole Hannah-Jones nearly broke the internet with a viral New York Times essay about sending her daughter to one of New York City’s worst-performing schools. While many of her conclusions drew criticism from education experts, there is one point on which Kelsey Piper found herself in firm agreement: Schools around the country are making it more and more difficult for parents to actually evaluate their children’s academic performance — and it’s not only because of grade inflation.

The Argument also released its latest national survey, which focused on how American voters think about war. Lakshya Jain, our director of political data, introduced the findings by highlighting just how incredibly unpopular Trump’s Iran war is with our respondents. Our polling shows that it’s nearly as unpopular as the Vietnam War, which killed over 58,000 Americans. And it’s even less popular than George W. Bush’s invasion of Iraq.

As a liberal, it’s tempting to stay out of public debates about the ultimate ends of human life. Liberal societies need to be able to accommodate private religious and spiritual codes that promote competing visions on this front. But in evading these questions, do we end up ceding ground to those who would degrade not just the political processes we value, but also the moral systems we privately hold dear? In his column this week, Matt Yglesias argues that while liberalism should remain neutral, liberals themselves need to take a stand on bigger questions than they may be comfortable with.

🌟Abundance Wins of the Week🌟

  • Top Senate Democrats and Republicans released the long-awaited text of a massive reform to the federal permitting regime: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAJAA). If passed, the package would make it much easier to build energy projects of all types — but likely with particularly pronounced benefits for clean energy — plus the long-distance transmission needed to efficiently move energy across the country.

  • In other good climate news, the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) issued a construction permit for the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) to build America’s first commercial small modular nuclear reactor. It’s the NRC’s second approval of construction for a new reactor this year, and both reviews were completed months ahead of schedule. Small modular reactors promise much simpler and faster paths to carbon-free nuclear energy than traditional reactors. (TVA will still need a separate operating license before it can run the reactor.)

  • New York City just unveiled 12 “Fast Track Districts” where it will streamline the review process for qualifying affordable housing projects. The districts — which include Manhattan’s Upper East and Upper West Sides, as well as large swaths of South Brooklyn, Staten Island, and Queens — were selected because they have produced the smallest share of the city’s affordable housing over the past five years: just 1% combined. The fast track process, which was approved by the city’s voters last year, is projected to reduce review times from seven months to three.

    Subscribe now

Worth watching…

There is a spectre haunting Europe: The far-right is on the rise. The AfD just placed first in the Saxony-Anhalt state elections in Germany. Reform UK is projected to come second in the next British general election. France will elect a new president next year, and the polling suggests that Marine Le Pen (or her acolyte Jordan Bardella) is the favorite to win.

Why is this happening? Is it the refusal of the center-left to make compromises on immigration? Or is it the refusal of the left to let people have air conditioning? Matt and Jerusalem discuss all this and more in the latest episode of The Argument podcast.

The only independent in the House of Representatives is waging a lonely fight against the gerrymandering arms race, which both political parties have escalated this cycle. Rep. Kevin Kiley, a former Republican who recently left the party after his district was redrawn, spoke with Lakshya Jain, The Argument’s director of political data, and Zachary Donnini about his decision and the polarization that gerrymandering encourages. “If you fight fire with fire, then the whole world burns,” he said. “There’s absolutely no reason that you should deprive your own citizens of fair representation based upon what some other state is doing.”

What’s News with The Argument

The Argument recommends, by Milan Singh

It’s officially October, and I’m ready for it: no more humidity, layering of outfits, assorted pumpkin spice foods and beverages. What can I say? I’m a bit basic.

To celebrate the arrival of autumn, I asked my esteemed colleagues for their fall-themed recommendations.

“I have no justification for how this is fall themed, but a friend found me in a Little Free Library The Floating Admiral, a detective novel collaboratively written by Agatha Christie, GK Chesterton, and twenty of their Golden Age detective novelist friends,” said staff writer Kelsey Piper. “It was great fun, and now I’m suffering immensely from the fact no one else I know has read it so that I can complain about it with them, so if you have read it, hit me up!”

Kelsey also read John LeCarre’s The Constant Gardener, but “while I love John LeCarre for being the most cynical everything-is-bad-because-of-human-nature-and-always-will-be spy novelist of them all, it hits differently when he’s being cynical about post-colonial Kenya instead of declining imperial Britain, so it was mostly just kind of depressing.”

Gender and culture fellow Maibritt Henkel recommended Julia Jacklin’s new album The Gem, which she said was “perfect for October — think Australian Phoebe Bridgers.” Operations manager Angela Tracy overcame some initial difficulty in narrowing the recommendations down (because “fall is the best time of year,” which is clearly true) but eventually settled on an unconventional-yet-simple dessert: a brûléed squash or sweet potato, riffing on the traditional Japanese winter snack.

The rest of the office was feeling a bit laconic, so I provided some additional incentive by telling them that if they didn’t give me a recommendation, I would have AI do it for them. That seemed to do the trick.

“This might make me sound like a narcissist but I randomly came across this book called Jerusalem the Golden by Margaret Drabble and immediately picked it up for obvious reasons,” said editor Jerusalem Demsas. “It’s a coming-of-age novel about a girl trying to break out of a provincial and constrained upbringing — but she finds out that no matter how far you run you can never escape your mother.”

“AI recommended that I recommend The Heart is a Lonely Hunter and I do, in fact, recommend it,” said senior editor John Thomason of Carson McCullers’s 1940 debut novel. “Alongside Ross McElwee’s 1986 film Sherman’s March, it’s probably the best piece of narrative art ever produced at least partially in (and, I would argue, at least partially by) Charlotte, North Carolina, a city with a well-known reputation for philistinism.”4

Video producer Justin Zuckerman also agreed with AI’s suggested recommendation: Ken Burns’ Baseball, which he’s about halfway through. “It’s around 18 hours of baseball history and lore, with folksy music and even folksier characters! It’s a great way to get excited about the postseason and also get your baseball fix during the winter months.”

Staff Writer Jeremiah Johnson said that he and his wife enjoyed watching “spoopy” — as in, “a mix of spooky and cute,” like The Nightmare Before Christmas — in the lead-up to Halloween.

“All horror media is implicitly fall-themed,” copy editor and fact checker Eli Richman noted, “and since he was robbed in The New York Times' top TV show list, I'll go ahead and recommend the works of Mike Flanagan. All of them…. The Haunting of Hill House gets all the love, and it's hard to argue it isn't deserved. But I'd reserve my biggest praise for Midnight Mass and Before I Wake.”
