item.title: The selfish war doctrine
item.content:encoded:
By Jeremiah Johnson

Welcome back to The Argument’s poll series, where we survey Americans on the issues everyone’s fighting about. Our full crosstabs are available behind the paywall at the end of this post. Our last surveys have asked about elite perception, AI, crime, gender issues, and much more.

You can see every single poll published by The Argument here.

Our full methodology can be read here.

—

Accepting his party’s nomination at the 2024 Republican National Convention, President Donald Trump promised that “the years of war, weakness, and chaos will be over” if he were elected.

He repeated some variation of this line dozens of times on the campaign trail. At a Bitcoin conference that same summer, he said, “I will end the endless wars. They never stop. Again, we had no wars. We had no new wars under your favorite president, President Trump. We had no new wars.”

Trump surrogates made the same argument frequently, as when former Democratic Rep. Tulsi Gabbard endorsed Trump, claiming that “[Trump] not only didn’t start any new wars, he took action to de-escalate and prevent wars” during his first term.

The standard story accepted by many pundits says that the GOP used to promote a more hawkish and pro-intervention foreign policy, but that Trump turned it into a more antiwar party — at least before he got bogged down in Iran (perhaps at the behest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu). The problem with this story is that it appears not to be true.

Trump has changed the right’s understanding of what American power is for. Bush-era Republicans paired their willingness to wage war with a belief that America should spread democracy, rebuild the countries it invaded, and sustain an international order. Trump rejected those obligations but retained the appetite for force — in his view, military action should deliver concrete gains for America, without saddling the nation with responsibilities to anyone else.

Subscribe now

In The Argument‘s new polling conducted Sept. 16-22, Republican voters share the president’s outlook: They remain enthusiastic about military action even as they distrust alliances and international institutions. That combination helps explain why a party that rejected Bush’s foreign policy still backs Trump’s war in Iran. The Republicans aren’t suddenly antiwar, they’re against liberal internationalism.

Though most Americans think the current war in Iran was a mistake, a strong majority of conservatives (61%) think it was right for the U.S. to start the war.

Whether you’re looking at 2024 Trump voters, self-identified conservatives, or Republicans, the story is roughly the same: Just over 60% support the current war in Iran. The narrative that Trump is betraying his base simply doesn’t match the polling data.

The right is also more likely than the left to approve of war in general and in a wide variety of scenarios. We asked poll respondents about past wars, and Republicans viewed America’s wars in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Vietnam far more favorably than Democrats did. Despite Trump’s criticism, a clear majority of Republicans still think it was correct to invade Iraq!

We also polled a number of hypothetical scenarios to decipher when voters think the U.S. is justified in taking military action. In every single scenario polled, a majority of Republicans said that military action was either always or usually justified — including a scenario where the action is just to promote America’s economic interests. And Republicans were more likely to approve of military action than Democrats in every scenario.

Trump has, of course, been more than happy to take military action in his second term. He sent special operations forces into Venezuela to kidnap the country’s dictator, Nicolas Maduro, and the administration has killed over 200 people in an ongoing series of military strikes, begun about a year ago, on alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean. Last spring, he began an extensive bombing campaign of Houthi rebels in Yemen, striking the group more than 1,100 times and killing hundreds. All this was before he unilaterally launched a war on Iran in an attempt to overthrow the country’s government.

Now that the Iran war is dragging into its ninth month, many onetime Trump supporters have turned on him, seeing it as a betrayal. Joe Rogan lamented that “no one thought that we were gonna go into this prolonged war with Iran,” while Tucker Carlson radiated a sense of betrayal, calling the war “absolutely disgusting and evil.”

Trump, it turns out, hasn’t changed the Republican Party in the way many people assumed he had. So how did we get here?

The anti-war presidency that wasn’t

The easiest way to unpack this paradox is to realize that Trump did change Republican foreign policy — just not in the ways that people usually assume. I think it’s true that the political right in the Trump era is considerably more skeptical of military entanglements than the old neoconservative establishment was. But they’re not skeptical at all of using force.

Former President George W. Bush didn’t invade Iraq merely to stop a threat to the United States. His administration was committed to the project of nation-building and the idea of spreading democracy abroad, which is part of how U.S. forces ended up spending so many years in both Iraq and Afghanistan. However poorly those military adventures may have turned out, Bush-era Republican leaders took seriously the idea that American power came with great obligations. They believed in rebuilding countries America invaded, supporting the new governments, and constructing an international order that would promote liberal democracy.

Trump is allergic to the very idea of such obligations. He views international affairs as a zero-sum contest. In the 2015 speech announcing his candidacy, Trump said the U.S. had spent $2 trillion on Iraq, lost thousands of lives, and gotten “nothing,” while claiming he had warned: “Don’t hit Iraq,” because it would “totally destabilize the Middle East.” He would later repeatedly criticize the war, calling it a horrible decision and a “big, fat mistake.”1

Trump’s main criticism of the war in Iraq was that it cost the U.S. an enormous amount of money and lives and we didn’t get anything out of it, which is why he often advocated for seizing Iraq’s oil. “Take the oil” was a Trump obsession for decades before he entered public office — he advocated taking Iran’s oil by force all the way back in 1987. His fixation on using foreign policy to seize resources is also why he cut an oil deal with the new Venezuelan leadership after kidnapping Maduro.

In a major 2016 speech, Trump promised that America was getting out of the nation-building business. But in that same speech, he promised unquestioned American military dominance and said that the world is most peaceful “when America is strongest.”

The Republican base seems to agree with him. For decades, Republicans were more likely than Democrats to say that the U.S. should take an active role in world affairs. But that number has reversed in recent years, with the major flip happening in 2016 as Trump was running for president. In 2023, only 47% of Republicans agreed the U.S. should take an active role, compared with 70% of Democrats.

As we can see above, that decline isn’t driven by the Republican base suddenly becoming skeptical of war overall. Instead, it appears that conservatives are simply less likely to believe in the idea of international obligations. Republican support for the 2015 Paris Agreement on climate change declined after Trump’s first election, Republican support for defending South Korea has declined, and a growing share of Republicans also believe that America’s security alliances with European nations provide no benefits.

This skepticism is reflected in The Argument’s recent polling questions on attitudes toward NATO and the U.N., which finds that Republicans are far less favorably inclined towards international institutions than Democrats.

Trump doesn’t dislike military action. He just hates the idea that America might undertake such actions for any purpose higher than self-interest. If there’s a Trump doctrine, it’s a selfish war doctrine: Do what’s best for me. Show strength at all times. Don’t let allies, enemies, or anyone else take advantage of you. Don’t get bogged down by treaties or obligations, but make sure that other countries are terrified of what might happen if they cross you.

The median Republican seems to have absorbed this lesson. They’re still far more likely to favor military actions than Democrats — whether past, current, or hypothetical future actions. But they distrust our alliances, dislike international agreements, and don’t want to be burdened or constrained by formal commitments.

In the end, Trump didn’t dislodge the right’s hawkishness, but he did transform it. Republicans are now less interested in maintaining the world and more interested in dominating it, less willing to accept long-term obligations, but still eager to swing the biggest stick.

This leaves the Republican Party in a difficult position.The party’s base seems to fundamentally agree with the Trump doctrine of selfish war, but the Iran war is deeply unpopular with both liberals and moderates. And the war’s popularity continues to drop as it drags out longer and longer, leading to increases in fuel prices and the cost of living that the public directly blames on the war. Add those factors together, and it’s a major reason why the midterms are shaping up to be a disaster for the GOP.

item.title: What if dictators never died?
item.description: I don't want to live forever but I'll take 150 years
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

This week on The Argument podcast, Matt Yglesias and I are joined by ChinaTalk’s Jordan Schneider to discuss all things China and AI. Paid subscribers can watch or listen to the episode ad free here and read the transcript at the end of this post. Free subscribers can watch the episode on YouTube here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Can we cure human frailty?

As we discover treatments for various diseases that used to reliably cut us down, humans are living longer than ever. The real question is whether curing all diseases would mean we get to live forever.

Before doing research for this essay, I believed that sometimes people just died of old age — that is, the human body is frail and just sort of stops working. That could mean cells stop replicating or become less functional, tissue loses its ability to repair everyday damage, or some other breakdown.

However, I was surprised to learn that there’s a lot of controversy over this common intuition.

Share

“Do centenarians die healthy?” is a study of 40 very old people. Researchers conducted autopsies to determine if there was some hidden cause of death, even if the deceased was described as healthy beforehand. In every single case, the doctors were able to attribute death to disease — usually cardiovascular or respiratory conditions. It’s not certain that those diseases were the cause of death, but it does cast doubt on the accepted folk wisdom about death from old age. Several independent autopsy studies found a similar pattern.

It seems at least theoretically possible to achieve immortality by preventing all diseases and replacing organs as they fail — though that proposition will get increasingly difficult as transplants extend to brains.

Actual immortality may be unlikely, but could humans eventually figure out how to keep our bodies going for a couple hundred years? That seems entirely plausible — but a world in which people can live for centuries is also one in which dictators can rule for centuries.

The undead dictator

Immortality may be the last thing you want to hear a dictator contemplate, but last year, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were overheard on a hot mic discussing just that.

“Before it’s said to be very rare to live up to 70, and now it’s said that you are still a child at 70,” said Xi (through an interpreter).

“In a few decades, as biotechnology continues to develop, human organs will continue to be transplanted and people will become younger and perhaps even achieve immortality,” noted Putin, also through an interpreter.

Xi later mused on predictions that humans “may be able to live up to 150 years old.”

World leaders are getting older. This is in part a function of aging electorates, but one report by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development showed that in autocracies, leaders were 26 years older than the median adult in 2023, compared to just 19 years in 1960. (Democracies saw no meaningful change.)

The explanation centers on turnover: The average tenure for an autocrat rose from roughly four years to over 10 over the last century, whereas for democratic leaders, tenure has fallen.

Recently, Xi came to Washington to meet with President Donald Trump. While little of substance seems to have emerged, ChinaTalk’s Jordan Schneider joined the latest episode of The Argument podcast to discuss the visit and its implications.

One takeaway was the visual evidence of human frailty on display between the two leaders: “Two most powerful countries in the world are ruled by one guy who’s 73 and one guy who’s 80. And they kind of don’t walk great anymore and need naps,” said Schneider.

When the end of one life feels like the end of history

There are many reasons the West rejected authoritarian governing models, but one core reason is that even if you get a very good king, there’s always the problem of succession.1

Aristotle questioned, “even if one held that royal government is best for states, what is to be the position as regards the king’s children?” After praising Rome’s comparatively good emperors, Edward Gibbon, in his canonical work The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, observed: “They must often have recollected the instability of a happiness which depended on the character of a single man.”

Natural death is a stabilizing force. For hungry would-be leaders waiting in the wings, the inevitable death of the leader reduces the incentive for assassination.

Subscribe now

We see a version of this dynamic mirrored in democracies as well — particularly in the “gerontocracy” discourse. As the average age of tenured faculty and politicians in key leadership roles has gone up, those waiting in the wings have grown increasingly restless. American universities removed mandatory retirement policies for tenured faculty in 1994, which sharply reduced retirement rates. As Yale Law professor Samuel Moyn characterized the situation, “younger academics today regard those elders much as serfs on the brink of the French Revolution saw the noble lords.” (A bit hyperbolic, but I take his core point.)

In 2018, a rebellion of young House Democrats led by Reps. Seth Moulton and Tim Ryan was trying to prevent then-78-year-old Nancy Pelosi’s return as speaker. In order to gain support, Pelosi acquiesced to term limits and described herself as the “bridge to the next generation of leaders.”

Natural death is also a solution for the subjects of tyrants. Revolt and exit are costly and sometimes ineffective — but if your autocrat is old enough, maybe you can just wait him out. Two of the worst dictators of the 20th century, Mao Zedong and Joseph Stalin, died to their nations’ great relief.

Ismikhan Rahimov, an Azerbaijani teacher sentenced to 25 years in the Gulag, later told his story in a magazine, writing that he held onto the expectation of Stalin’s death:

“I was convinced that as soon as Stalin died, a new policy would take effect in Russia. That’s the way it had always been throughout Russia’s entire history. When the Czar was overthrown, a new policy was established. Besides, Stalin was already 70 years old at the time I was arrested. I knew his end was coming. So I knew that we would come back. Little did I know, however, how long it would take, and what difficult circumstances I would have to live through, until that day.”

One month after Mao’s death in 1976, his successors arrested Mao’s proteges — the Gang of Four — marking the end of the Cultural Revolution. They were charged with many crimes that Mao himself was also responsible for, including “keeping a nation of 800 million living in constant fear” and “ruining the education system” and “preventing a single poem or play from being printed much less published without their approval.”

In many ways, they were forced to pay for their own crimes as well as Mao’s.

The Chinese Communist Party’s 1981 historical resolution acknowledged Mao’s ultimate responsibility, but immediately after doing so, it argued that Mao’s dark age was “the error of a great proletarian revolutionary.” While the chairman “paid constant attention to overcoming shortcomings in the life of the Party and state,” late in life he “confused right and wrong and the people with the enemy.”

Meanwhile, the Gang of Four were accused of “taking advantage of Comrade Mao Zedong’s errors [and] committ[ing] many crimes behind his back, bringing disaster to the country and the people.” Mao’s death gave his successors room to abandon some of his most disastrous policies while continuing to celebrate him as a great revolutionary.

While Mao’s death famously did not pave the road to democracy in China, there are more hopeful examples. According to one historian, opposition to Francisco Franco’s dictatorial regime in Spain was willing to wait for Franco’s death, much to the chagrin of young Basque activists. Franco’s opponents could hope to outlast him even if they could not overthrow him. That calculation looks very different if a dictator can expect another century in power.

Of course, death is not a panacea.

Many dictators die, and their countries fall into chaos and civil war or peacefully transition to another dictator. But a dictator’s death does create an opening to escape that particular ruler’s regime.

Share

Some autocrats are in fact better than others. China is not some paragon of liberalism and democracy, but life for everyday people became substantially better after Mao’s death — political persecution declined significantly and Deng Xiaoping’s eventual ascendancy ushered in an era of economic growth that raised living standards more than any other event in human history.

Do you want to live forever?

Dictators are a highly selected bunch and probably score higher in areas like megalomania than the rest of us — but nevertheless, I am curious how readers of The Argument score on whether or not they want to live forever!

In a 2015 YouGov poll of British adults, just 28% of people said they would like to live forever if they could. In a 2025 Pew poll, Americans were asked how long they would live if they could choose, and the average age was 91; just 7% said they would like to live to 120 or beyond. (Forever was not offered as an option.)

Part of what’s going on here is that some people don’t want to live a long time if they’re living diminished lives in poor health. Another is that one’s friends and family don’t always get to come along. Other survey evidence indicates that if one or both of those matters were squared away, higher numbers of people would take the longevity pill.

An extra century with the people you love seems great — as long as it’s not another century under autocratic rule.

Today’s podcast with Schneider and my co-host Matt Yglesias ranges far afield from longevity. We get into how Chinese and American political leaders are using AI and how the technology is shaping geopolitical crises. It’s a really fun episode, and it’s great to have a bona fide expert on to gab with us about geopolitics.

Download wherever you get your podcasts!

The Argument. Libbing out.

Paying subscribers can find the transcript for this post beneath the paywall.

Subscribe now

New episodes post every Thursday.

For an ad-free version and full transcript, subscribe at TheArgumentMag.com.

Corrections and clarifications:

  • Around 21:35, Jordan references the “seven other parties in China.” There are eight subordinate satellite parties in China in addition to the CCP.

  • Around 26:15, Jordan says China was growing at a rate of 8% to 9% in the 2000s, 5% to 6% in the 2010s, and between 0.5% and 1.5% for the past six years. According to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, the country grew at a rate of 8.3% to 14.2% in the 2000s, 6.1% to 10.6% in the 2010s, and 2.3% to 8.6% in the 2020s.

  • Around 27:50, Jordan says the U.S. has an unemployment rate of 3%. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ latest report, the unemployment rate reached 4.2% in September.

  • Around 49:40, Jordan suggests 50 million people died in the Chinese Cultural Revolution. According to scholar Song Yongyi, estimates range from 500,000 to 8 million.

  • Around 1:04:00, Jordan says AI is polling at 14%. A July 2026 survey by HarrisX showed 56% of U.S. voters with a favorable view of AI. The Argument has not polled this question specifically, but in Sept. 2025, 43% of voters said AI has had a positive impact on their own life and 32% said it has a positive impact on society. In July 2026, 55% said they at least somewhat enjoyed using AI.

item.title: The MAGA realignment realigns
item.description: The numbers behind the Trump coalition’s crackup
item.content:encoded:
By Lakshya Jain

To virtually anyone watching the 2024 election, one of the biggest shocks of the cycle was the way young and Hispanic voters zoomed toward Donald Trump.

Two years later, it’s difficult to find signs of the president retaining any of that once-mythical strength.

Share

Through aggregating and analyzing the surveys we’ve done at The Argument, we have been able to reconstruct a spectacularly detailed picture of both the American electorate at large and the likely electorate of 2026. This trove of data allows us to see Trump’s approval and voting intent for each subgroup. And it tells us that Democrats are making titanic gains among the groups they initially lost ground with in 2024, as young and Hispanic voters abandon Trump at dizzying speeds.

Whether because of disillusionment over his foreign policy, anger over his immigration agenda, or disappointment over the way he has handled the cost-of-living crisis, Trump’s approval has cratered spectacularly. His net approval with Hispanic voters sits at -37 with registered voters, and at -39 with likely voters. Meanwhile, the picture is even uglier with young voters, as his approval sits at a shocking -45 with registered voters and -50 with likely ones.

Two things are happening as a result. First, a lot of voters are simply switching sides. Among all registered voters between 2024 and 2026, Democrats have gained over 11 percentage points of margin with Hispanics and young voters alike, which exceeds the leftward national swing by a few points.

But our polling also found something else: a lot of the conservative voters who remain unwilling to vote for Democrats are also so angry at Trump that they have no intention of showing up in 2026. We see this in the delta between the likely voter electorate and the registered-voter electorate. Even though registered voters are a less Democratic sample, Trump’s approval is the same in both groups. That means the registered voters who are unlikely to vote are disproportionately Republican-leaning voters who disapprove of Trump.1 This takes the swings projected for the midterm from notable to colossal.

When we compared the margins of the 2024 election to those of the likely 2026 electorate, Democrats picked up 17 percentage points in net margin with Hispanics, as well as 23 points with voters under the age of 30.

In the case of Hispanics, these projected 2026 margins are on par with Joe Biden’s 2020 numbers.2 Meanwhile, with young voters, you’d have to go back to either the 2018 blue wave or Barack Obama’s 2008 landslide for the last time Democrats saw numbers this high.

Subscribe now

It would be a mistake to look at this and think that the Democratic problems of 2024 are all solved. Voters who sit out the 2026 midterms may return for the 2028 presidential election. And among all registered voters — not just the ones likely to vote this November — the shift toward Democrats is considerably smaller, even though Trump is similarly unpopular in both groups. That suggests a substantial and disproportionate chunk of the voters who have abandoned the president remain unwilling to vote for Democrats.

In particular, when it comes to the full electorate of registered voters, the margin by which people disapprove of Trump is much larger than Democrats’ lead over Republicans. That gap is especially large with many subgroups, including young and white noncollege voters, suggesting again that dissatisfaction with Trump doesn’t necessarily translate into votes for Democrats.

That’s the sort of thing that calls into question just how durable either side’s electoral position really is. It means that these voters remain up for grabs in the next election despite how intensely they’ve soured on the president, giving both sides glimmers of hope in 2028. After all, while it’s clear that most voters now dislike Trump, it’s not yet so clear that they would vote for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, or Kamala Harris over Secretary of State Marco Rubio or Vice President JD Vance in 2028.

When I see the chart we’ve assembled above, I see a myriad of potential outcomes.

In one, Democrats could sweep 2028 in the same way that they dominated 2008. Disillusioned white working-class voters, Hispanics, and young voters could rocket to the left over disappointment with the outgoing Republican president’s handling of foreign wars, cost of living, and healthcare.

In another, a tight election could result in a narrow Republican win, with just enough voters holding their nose for a different kind of Republican candidate against an unappealing Democrat.

Those are two wildly different outcomes, but in many ways, the uncertainty is the point. Though the story of 2026 may be largely written by now, the story of 2028 certainly isn’t.

But this is still a very different type of discussion than the one we were having in 2024. Axios‘ youth-vote analysis declared, “A big chunk of the future electorate is MAGA red” and claimed “lasting power” for MAGA. Data scientist David Shor, speaking on The Ezra Klein Show, described young people as “potentially the most conservative generation that we’ve experienced maybe in 50 to 60 years.” Few predicted that the right-wing youth revolution of 2024 was potentially just a blip on the radar.

Meanwhile, endless pages of ink were spilled on the loss of Democratic standing with Hispanics. Discussing Republican gains in heavily Hispanic communities, pollster Patrick Ruffini argued that “the FDR coalition is being dismantled piece by piece and being reassembled in Donald Trump’s GOP.”

The change we’re seeing doesn’t make those autopsies any less correct or valuable, but it does remind us that the certainty can sometimes just be an artifact of a lack of data. With two years between elections, each race is analyzed and scrutinized endlessly with a fine-toothed comb in the hopes of avoiding or predicting the next surprise.

But at the end of the day, the choices that parties make really do matter. And had Trump made some different ones, we probably wouldn’t be having this conversation today.

Subscribe now

METHODOLOGY

To assemble these estimates, we combined data from all of the surveys performed by The Argument over the course of 2026. First, a likely voter screen was created for each survey. The likely voter screen takes every respondent’s demographic and voting history and calculates a probability that they will vote in 2026. It then aligns this with probabilistic turnout scores from self-expressed vote likelihood and rakes this to the likely 2026 electorate, calculated via historical demographic turnout data from a Catalist voter file sample, in order to estimate respondents’ likelihood of voting.

Then, the pooled survey file is fitted among 2024 voters to have demographic shares and Verasight panel-profiled votes match the margins in Catalist’s 2024 What Happened report on the following factors: race by age, race by education, and race by gender (for white, Black, and Hispanic voters). It is also weighted to match the report’s margins for age and to match the actual, certified election results by region. This allows us to anchor our own 2026 estimates by ensuring that the 2024 vote margins of our demographics align with actual, validated external measures. Every registered voter is also weighted to the Catalist voter file sample’s benchmarks on white/nonwhite by modeled party.

Respondent likely voter weights are then rescaled by the amount they shifted by during the recalled margin rake, and the likely electorate is then restratified across demographics to align with the initial likely electorate screen.

Recommended reading:

1

It’s especially notable that Trump’s approval is better among the likely electorate than the full electorate of registered voters for noncollege whites.

2

It should be noted, though, that these are still well short of the margins that Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton put up.
